s: A site for the hydrogen bomb
t: In June 1950, with war begun in Korea, the Atomic Energy Commission enlarged the job it was asking Du Pont to take on: three more heavy-water reactors, five in all (WB: SRS at Fifty ch. 7).

s: A site for the hydrogen bomb
t: Du Pont surveyed candidate sites and settled on the middle Savannah River in South Carolina, a tract big enough to hold an exclusion zone around the reactors (WB: ch. 7). DOE's own timeline dates President Truman's letter to Du Pont to 20 October 1950 (WB: DOE, energy.gov/srs).

s: A site for the hydrogen bomb
t: The announcement came at noon on 28 November 1950: about 250,000 acres in Aiken and Barnwell counties, to be called the Savannah River Plant, designed, built and operated by Du Pont (WB: SRS at Fifty ch. 8). The next morning it was in the Atlanta Constitution (IA) and, by wire, in papers as far away as Victoria, British Columbia (IA).

The land was not empty. Ellenton, with about 600 people, and Dunbarton, with 231, stood inside the boundary, along with Meyers Mill, Jackson, Hawthorne, Robbins, Leigh, Snelling and Hattieville (WB: ch. 7). Most of the farms were worked by tenants, and most of the agricultural workforce was African American (WB: ch. 7).

How many people were moved depends on who is counting. The first press release spoke of about 1,500 families; early reports said up to 8,000 farmers; the AEC settled on 6,000 people in 1,500 families (WB: ch. 8). The Savannah River Archaeological Research Program later put it at about 5,000 (WB: SRARP).

The Army Corps of Engineers ran the acquisition. Residents of the first area had to be gone by 15 March 1951 and of the second by 1 June; owners who disputed an appraisal went to federal condemnation proceedings; at least 4,500 graves had to be moved (WB: ch. 8). By late 1951 the government was acquiring 265 tracts in Ellenton alone (DL).

Owners objected to how their land was bought. A congressional staff report in late 1951 found Ellenton residents told to be gone by February 1952 while their property was still unappraised, each owner given a single offer at the appraised value, and those who took the first offer as much as 20 percent worse off than those who held out; about a hundred owners met twice to protest the prices.

The Atomic Energy Commission answered that most condemnations came from defects in title rather than price, though it conceded that juries in seven contested cases had awarded substantially more than the government's appraisal (DL).

The Reporter told the national story in March 1951 as the quiet doom of Ellenton (IA). Jet told a different part of it that December: Black families moving whole houses fifteen miles to New Ellenton, the replacement town (IA). A 1965 federal housing study counted about 30 white and 120 Black families relocated near New Ellenton (IA), and by 1953 Congress was hearing that New Ellenton had been left out of aid it needed (DL).

The displaced spoke for themselves decades later, in oral histories collected from 1990 and published as Memories of Home for Ellenton and for Dunbarton and Meyers Mill (WB: OSTI 272945; WB: OSTI 10171577). The program's web pages and the chapter PDFs survive in Wayback; srarp.org itself is gone (WB; WB: Ellenton volume).

James McBride's life of James Brown touches on the Black sharecroppers forced out of Ellenton (IA). Louise Cassels's The Unexpected Exodus (1971), the classic memoir of the leaving, is catalogued in Open Library, though it has no copy to read or borrow yet (OL: Open Library).

Construction began in 1951 — the R reactor in June, P in July, L in October, by the Natural Resources Defense Council's count (IA). The Bureau of Labor Statistics followed the work force in a four-part study in 1952 (IA: part I). It records Black tenant farmers arriving in Augusta looking for jobs in May 1951, and an NAACP meeting in Aiken that September charging Du Pont over its hiring.

Getting hired was a fight of its own. In November 1951 a House labor subcommittee under Graham Barden held five days of hearings in Augusta on charges that union membership had become a condition of work (DL).

Its report the next year found that Du Pont hired manual labor through a verbal understanding with the AFL building-trades unions, turning job seekers away at the gate, and that Atomic Energy Commission officials had either approved or failed to find out (DL). In November 1952 pickets from an AFL engineers' union nearly stopped construction, with about 25,000 other workers honoring the line (IA).

The same system kept Black workers out of the skilled trades. The National Urban League's field notes, filed with the Barden hearings, record that it pressed Du Pont in August 1951 over its failure to hire Black electricians, mechanics, plumbers, welders and ironworkers, and that company officials replied they would use no source but the unions while the unions could supply the labor, and would give no figures for Black employment beyond carpenters (DL). When Truman created a committee on government contract compliance that December, Jet expected the Savannah River contractors to be among its first targets (IA).

Housing the workers was its own crisis. Congress held a hearing in Aiken in February 1951 that expected the construction peak around the start of 1953 (DL), and by February 1952 the mayors of New Ellenton and Augusta were testifying about dormitories and Du Pont's part in housing (DL).

House & Home reported about 4,000 trailers for married workers (IA). The housing builder later sued Du Pont in a case that reached the Supreme Court (DL), and South Carolina's attempt to tax Du Pont's work on the plant set out what a government-owned, contractor-operated plant was in law (DL).

Du Pont wrote its own record of all this, volume by volume, in construction and design histories now on OSTI (WB: OSTI 10159481; EXT: OSTI 10151705). The company's administrative files are at the Hagley Museum and Library, by DOE's own finding aid (WB: DOE OHRE).

Hagley's guide to its Atomic Energy Division records, 80 linear feet from 1942 to 1989, describes a Savannah River Project series covering site selection, design and construction, environment and community impact, safety and waste disposal (WB: Hagley finding aid). Its photograph collection for the plant, 1951 to 1984, holds 1,412 prints and 388 lantern slides (WB: Hagley finding aid).

The 305-M test pile was the first reactor to go critical on the site, in 1952, the year heavy-water production began in D Area (WB: srs.gov 1950s). R reactor went critical in December 1953, P on 20 February 1954, and all five were running by the end of March 1955 (WB: SRS at Fifty ch. 11).

The F Area separations plant started in 1954 and H Area in 1955; tritium went to the AEC from 1955; the basic plant was complete in 1956 (WB: srs.gov 1950s; WB: History Highlights). The first shipment of plutonium is dated December 1954 by one official source and 1955 by others (WB: ch. 11; WB).

In 1956 the neutrino was confirmed at P reactor. R and the heavy-water components test reactor shut down in 1964, and L in 1968 (WB: srs.gov 1960s). The standard history of the reactors is Carlisle and Zenzen's Supplying the Nuclear Arsenal (IA), and the South Carolina State Historic Preservation Office holds a long illustrated study of the five reactor areas (WB: SC SHPO).

The plant's own figures understated its early releases. The CDC's dose reconstruction found that the iodine-131 released to the air in the 1950s, mainly from the separations plants, was about four times what the site had reported, largely because its samplers caught only one chemical form of the iodine (WB: CDC dose reconstruction, Phase II ch. 1). The largest tritium releases to the air came in 1957–59 from the H Area tritium facilities (WB).

A fuel failure in R reactor in November 1957 sent more than 1,900 curies into a seepage basin dug only that year, and in 1958 three high-level waste tanks in H Area leaked through their steel walls (WB: CDC Phase II ch. 5).

The final report judged the doses to people living nearby small, but found that a child born in 1955 received much of a lifetime dose from the site in its first years, from those early iodine releases (WB: CDC Phase III).

On 14 March 1955, after a light rain, contamination across the plant set off the shoe monitors of workers coming in from outside. The plant blamed fallout from a bomb test in Nevada two days before. In 1985 Bernd Franke and Robert Alvarez argued that a reactor accident was the likelier source, since the contamination centred on the K, L and P reactors.

At Senator Thurmond's request, the staff of the Senate Armed Services Committee investigated and reported in July 1986 that their case was "merely speculative": the contamination matched fallout from the Teapot Hornet test, and the plant's own monitoring showed no release (DL). The CDC's contractor judged Nevada fallout highly probable, while noting that the full extent of the deposit would never be known (WB: CDC Phase II ch. 6).

The workers' side of the reckoning came later still. In 2012 the government added everyone who had worked at the site for at least 250 days between 1953 and 1972 to the Special Exposure Cohort under the federal occupational illness compensation program, so that their cancer claims no longer turn on reconstructing each worker's dose (WB: NIOSH).

Before the reactors ran, the river was surveyed. Ruth Patrick of the Academy of Natural Sciences made a baseline survey in 1951 (WB: srs.gov 1950s), and the Public Health Service sampled the river's water and its natural radioactivity in 1951–52 (IA; IA).

AEC officials approached Eugene Odum of the University of Georgia in 1951 to study the reservation's ecosystems (IA; IA). That work became a permanent laboratory in 1961 (WB: srs.gov 1960s) — the Savannah River Ecology Laboratory, which dates its own founding to 1951 (WB: SREL).

Through the 1970s the plant reported its releases. Du Pont's semiannual monitoring summaries were reprinted in the federal Radiation Data and Reports (DL), and its annual environmental reports run from 1974 on OSTI (WB: OSTI 4174736). In 1972 the plant became the first National Environmental Research Park (WB: srs.gov 1970s).

The ecology laboratory's work on reactor cooling water began in 1969, once satellite imagery had made the water temperatures impossible to keep secret (WB: Ecological Society of America), and became the Thermal Ecology symposia (IA). The first on-site anti-nuclear protest came in 1979 (WB: srs.gov 1970s).

Tritium was the plant's largest routine release, averaging more than half a million curies a year to the air in 1974–77 (WB: OSTI 6206385). Single accidents added to it. On 2 May 1974 some 479,000 curies of tritium gas escaped from a stack (WB: OSTI 7100365), a release a Lawrence Livermore report on the national emergency-response system's tracking of it called a small quantity, not dangerous to the public (WB: OSTI 7282426).
In September 1984 another 43,800 curies, mostly tritium oxide, drifted toward New Ellenton and Aiken (WB: OSTI 6417935), and on 31 July 1987 a further 172,000 curies were released (WB: OSTI 7130595).

Downstream, the plant tested the tritium in the drinking water of the Beaufort-Jasper Water Authority in South Carolina and the Port Wentworth plant in Georgia every month, and screened the 865 deer and 8 hogs killed in its 1971 hunt for cesium-137 before releasing them to hunters (DL).

The hunts go on: the site has opened them to the public every autumn since 1965, and every deer and hog killed is still checked for cesium-137, none released if it would take the hunter over the site's limit (WB: srs.gov, 2025; WB: srs.gov hunt rules).

The Reagan-era buildup needed more plutonium. In 1982 the plant lowered the Pu-240 content of its product to blend with Hanford's (WB: SRS at Fifty ch. 19), and DOE moved to restart L reactor, idle since 1968, on an environmental assessment rather than a full impact statement (WB: OSTI 5060401).

The Natural Resources Defense Council sued. On 15 July 1983 the district court held that the restart needed an environmental impact statement but would not stop it (EXT: Environmental Law Reporter). The Senate Armed Services Committee had already held a field hearing in North Augusta that February (DL).

There Georgia's Senator Mattingly, calling the Tuscaloosa aquifer under the site the main source of water for Georgia, won an assurance from DOE that burying the plant's high-level waste in the bedrock beneath it would not be brought up again, and the Natural Resources Defense Council's witness pointed to cesium contamination off the site, just downstream of where Steel Creek enters the river (DL).

South Carolina and Georgia had both opposed bedrock disposal (IA). The final EIS came in May 1984 (WB: DOE); it and the other impact statements of the period are gathered in one archive.org upload (IA). L restarted in 1985. C reactor shut down that year, permanently from 1986 (WB: srs.gov 1980s).

Outside critics read the record differently from the operator. Deadly Crop in the Tank Farm (1986) assessed the high-level waste tanks (WB: IEER); Du Pont published a rebuttal (WB: OSTI 5881523). The Washington Post described aging reactors carrying the buildup, one down for a cracked vessel — a clipping that survives in the CIA's files (IA).

What the plant had poured into its seepage basins came back through the groundwater. Reviewing permit applications in 1981, South Carolina's health and environment department judged that the volumes sent to the basins strongly suggested groundwater problems; in 1983 the plant reported that a well supplying drinking water to its own employees was contaminated, and two more followed.
The department's deputy commissioner told Senator Glenn's committee in 1987 that plant staff had at first been reluctant to accept the state's regulatory authority (DL).

GAO found solvents in the groundwater under the M Area fuel plant at more than 30,000 times proposed drinking-water standards and tritium at the separations areas at more than 2,500 times; DOE answered that the contamination stayed under federal land and posed no threat to the public (IA: GAO 1986).
By 1991 the Office of Technology Assessment reported an EPA finding that the pump-and-treat system meant to clean the M Area plume was not adequately designed to reach its goal (DL).

A National Academy of Sciences panel reviewed safety at the defense production reactors for DOE in 1987 (IA). Du Pont announced that year that it would not stay on as operator (WB: srs.gov 1980s). In February 1988 a Senate subcommittee heard DOE, the plant manager and Du Pont on why L reactor's power had been cut (IA).

That year an internal list of thirty significant reactor incidents became public. The official history presents the report as meant to show safety improving (WB: ch. 19); the Senate investigator who obtained it remembers it as evidence of concealment (WB: Alliance for Nuclear Accountability).

The reactors went down one after another — K in April, L in June, P in August — over emergency cooling concerns (WB: ch. 19). On 30 September 1988 the General Accounting Office told Senator Glenn's and Representative Synar's committees how P reactor's start-up had gone ahead despite a reactivity shortfall larger than any the plant had seen (DL; WB: gao.gov).

Glenn's bill to put the weapons plants under outside safety oversight was already in hearings (DL). The next day, 1 October, the New York Times put the story on its front page: severe accidents at the plant, kept secret for up to 31 years, at all five reactors, documented in a 19-page memorandum from a plant supervisor to his superiors at Du Pont (WB: New York Times). By November the paper was asking how Congress had missed the signs (WB: New York Times).

In April 1989 the Westinghouse Savannah River Company took over from Du Pont (WB: ch. 19). The same year the Savannah River Plant became the Savannah River Site and went on the National Priorities List (WB: srs.gov 1980s). GAO's 1989 testimony set the site inside a complex-wide picture of cleanup and modernization problems (DL).

That August Senator Glenn argued that DOE's research on the health of its own workers had been subordinated to production, and Senator Kohl called for removing the apparent conflict of interest and said he was open to moving that research to Health and Human Services; the record included a 1988 study reporting a significant excess of leukemia deaths among hourly Savannah River workers hired before 1955 (IA: Senate hearing, 1989). The later dose reconstruction was run by the CDC (WB: CDC).

DOE still meant to restart. In February 1991 it planned K for that summer and L for 1992, at $3.2 billion for restart and operations (WB: GAO RCED-91-95), and issued safety evaluations for K (WB: OSTI 5625511). In December 1991 tritium from K reactor reached the Savannah River (WB: OSTI 5281815; WB: OSTI 10179303).

GAO had warned in 1989 that DOE had only begun to address earthquake weaknesses that had existed at the site for years, and that the seismic review behind P reactor's 1988 restart used a less stringent standard than the Nuclear Regulatory Commission's (IA: GAO 1989).

In March 1991 a depression found on the downstream face of the Par Pond dam led the site to lower the reservoir about 19 feet that summer, exposing some 1,300 acres of cesium-contaminated sediment and sending tritium and cesium into the river (WB: OSTI 7247383); the exposed bed became a Superfund interim action (EXT: OSTI 10192315).
A 1998 DOE notice dates the leak to 1992 (DL). In 1992 K went critical for a test run and was then shut down permanently (WB: srs.gov 1990s). Bomb making at Savannah River was over.

What it had released was reconstructed later. The CDC's dose reconstruction counted about 3,000 release incidents involving tritium between 1954 and 1992 (WB: CDC Phase II); cdc.gov now refuses automated requests, and the reports are reachable in Wayback.

The official history marks the turn plainly: the mission became environmental management, not production (WB: SRS at Fifty ch. 20). DOE priced the complex-wide legacy in Estimating the Cold War Mortgage (IA) and traced each waste stream to the process that made it in Linking Legacies (IA). In October 2003 the last spent fuel left the receiving basin, closing what the site called a forty-year era (WB).

Spent fuel kept arriving as well as leaving. When the United States moved to take back the fuel it had supplied to research reactors abroad, GAO reported in 1994 that delays had already led reactors in Belgium and Germany to reprocess theirs, and that DOE meant to store the first returns at Savannah River (IA: GAO 1994).

DOE's 1996 decision accepted about 22,700 fuel elements from 41 countries over 13 years, most landing at the Charleston Naval Weapons Station, with the aluminum-based fuel all managed at Savannah River (DL: Federal Register, 1996). South Carolina's governor took DOE to court over it (DL).

The largest legacy was liquid: about 36 million gallons in 49 tanks, roughly 421 million curies (WB: DWPF fact sheet). The Defense Waste Processing Facility, built from 1983 and troubled before it ran (IA: GAO 1992), began turning that waste into glass on 12 March 1996 (WB).

Getting the waste into the glass plant was harder. The process DOE chose in 1983 to pull cesium out of the tanks' salt, In-Tank Precipitation, had been expected to cost $32 million and be finished by 1988; after about a decade and almost half a billion dollars it was abandoned in 1998 because it gave off large amounts of benzene (DL: House hearing, 2000; WB: GAO).

Its replacement, the Salt Waste Processing Facility, was to be built by 2008 for $900 million; in 2015 DOE's Inspector General reported about $1.4 billion in cost growth and a start no earlier than December 2018 (WB: DOE Inspector General). It poured its 4,000th canister on 31 December 2015, of about 8,000 expected (WB), and had passed 4,500 by its thirtieth anniversary in 2026 (WB).

Tanks 17 and 20 were closed in 1997, the first in the nation (WB). What could be left in the ground was settled by Section 3116 of the 2005 defense authorization act (WB: govinfo), which Senator Graham said he wrote and which passed by a single vote (WB), and which the National Academies reviewed for Savannah River (IA).
Tanks 18 and 19 followed in 2012 (WB), and in May 2026 Tank 14 became the eighth old-style tank to reach the end of waste removal in under two years (WB).

In 2018 and 2019 DOE reinterpreted "high-level waste" to turn on how radioactive a waste is rather than where it came from, revising the change after objections from the Nuclear Regulatory Commission, members of Congress and states. Savannah River was its first test: in 2020 DOE decided to send grouted wastewater from the glass plant to a commercial disposal site in Andrews, Texas, beginning with 8 gallons (WB: Federal Register; EXT: Federal Register).
In March 2008 the site put up South Carolina historic markers for P and R, the first inside the fence (WB). Then Recovery Act money arrived.

Deactivation of the R reactor building was cleared in March 2009 (WB); the reactors were sealed in place between October 2009 and September 2011 (WB: OSTI 1032952), five years ahead of the schedule without the stimulus (WB). The release marking the end of that work is gone from srs.gov; the Wayback capture is the copy (WB).

South Carolina's fight over plutonium began before MOX. In April 2002 DOE decided to store surplus plutonium from Rocky Flats at Savannah River. Governor Jim Hodges sued, then issued an executive order banning plutonium from the state's roads, and in June a federal court barred him from interfering with the shipments; the Fourth Circuit found that DOE had not broken environmental law (DL: Hodges v. Abraham). He had vowed to lie in the road to stop them (IA).

Congress spent a decade on turning surplus plutonium into reactor fuel at Savannah River (DL; DL). DOE's 2016 baseline put the mixed-oxide plant at $17.17 billion, finished in 2048 — a document since removed from the watchdog site that posted it (WB: SRS Watch).

South Carolina sued to hold the government to its promises (WB: complaint), and The Post and Courier's source documents on the fight are on archive.org (IA). In May 2018 DOE certified that diluting and disposing of the plutonium would cost less than half of finishing MOX; the Fourth Circuit lifted the injunction keeping the project alive on 8 January 2019 (WB: 4th Cir.).

MOX workers had already been offered a job fair in December 2018 (WB). By August 2019 DOE reported a metric ton of plutonium removed from the state (WB: SC Attorney General). Half of that ton had gone, secretly, to Nevada.

DOE announced in August 2018 that it planned to send up to a metric ton there; Nevada sued, and learned through the suit that DOE had already shipped half of it while seemingly negotiating in good faith. In a 2020 settlement DOE agreed to remove that half ton from Nevada by the end of 2026 and to send no more (WB: Nevada Attorney General).

The site was also offered other countries' material. In 2014 DOE began assessing whether to take Germany's spent pebble-bed reactor fuel, graphite spheres containing American-supplied highly enriched uranium (WB: Federal Register); the site's own Citizens Advisory Board voted against it in 2017 (WB: CAB), and by 2022 the German state concerned had chosen to store it at home instead (WB: SRS Watch).

Plutonium from a Japanese research assembly did come, through Charleston in 2016 (WB: SRS Watch), and in 2021 NNSA dropped its plan to send it on to New Mexico, deciding to process it at Savannah River and store it there until a geologic repository exists (EXT: Federal Register).

The site's weapons work has not ended with it. DOE decided in November 2020 to make plutonium pits at Savannah River (WB: Federal Register), and SRS Watch and others are challenging the decision in federal court (DL). Tritium work has continued throughout (WB).

In 2019 the Defense Nuclear Facilities Safety Board warned that a fire, crane drop or explosion in the tritium facilities could cause acute radiation sickness or death in a significant number of people (WB: Federal Register); NNSA's administrator replied, "I do not accept Recommendation 2019-2" (WB: Federal Register).

Compensation for the plant's sick workers came slowly. At a 2003 House hearing Representative Charlie Norwood of Georgia said more than 300 of his constituents had filed claims over work at the site and only a handful had a decision, and the building trades' statement called Savannah River workers treated unfairly under the program (DL: House hearing, 2003).

The 2012 class that spared early workers individual dose reconstruction was extended in 2021 to subcontracted construction workers through 1990 (WB: Federal Register) and in 2026 through 1993 (EXT: Federal Register).
The site's laboratory was named the country's newest national laboratory in 2004 (WB). Both SRNL.GOV and SRS.GOV have been archived via Archive-It since July 2023 (AIT: collection 21601).

The ecology laboratory fared worse. Its grant was cut 47 percent for 2006, with layoffs that September (WB: UGA); the next year's funding fell to $1 million against an expected $4.5 million, which the site's own Citizens Advisory Board called reprehensible (WB: SRS CAB).
The House Science Committee held a hearing on it in July 2007 (DL; video IA). SREL's web page from that summer mentions a statement on a budget crisis (WB) but the actual statement has been lost.

The SRS Museum opened in Aiken after a 2014 ribbon-cutting (WB); its website is dead but the Wayback Machine has the record (WB). The site's archaeologists and its Cold War historic preservation program work with it (WB) — the same program that collected Ellenton's memories in 1990.

The federal record of historic engineering holds one part of the plant in detail. The Historic American Engineering Record documented the Physics Assembly Laboratory in M Area, home of the zero-power Process Development Pile that set the physics for plutonium and tritium production in the five reactors, in 107 photographs and 123 data pages (WB: Library of Congress, HAER SC-43).
